name: Technical Debt and Refactoring
intent: Treat a shortcut in the code as a loan: it buys speed now and charges interest, in slower changes, on every later change in that code; repay it in small, tested steps where the interest is high, and leave it alone where it is not.
scenario: A team has 40 points of work per sprint and code with 30 points of debt. In code changed every sprint, a feature costs 10 points plus one for every 10 points of debt, and each rushed feature adds 2 more. The same team is run three ways over 6, 12 and 24 sprints: ignore the debt, spend 8 points a sprint on small refactoring steps (with and without tests), or stop and rewrite for 3, 6 or 12 sprints. Then the debt is placed in code nobody touches.
problem: Ward Cunningham's metaphor says that shipping code you know is imperfect is like borrowing money: fine if you repay it, costly if you do not. The cost is not the ugliness. It is the extra time every later change takes in that area, so it grows with how often the code is changed. Teams get this wrong in both directions. They never repay, and each feature gets slower; or they treat all untidy code as debt, refactor without a safety net, break behaviour, and propose a rewrite that stops delivery for months and ends with its own debt.

howItWorks.title: Name the kind of debt
howItWorks.text: Deliberate debt is a conscious trade: ship with a hard-coded rule to meet a date, and write down what the proper version would be. Accidental debt is found later, when you learn a better design than the one you built, or when the requirements shifted under it. Martin Fowler's quadrant adds prudent against reckless: a deliberate, written-down shortcut is a loan; skipping design because you could not be bothered is not a loan, it is a leak. Only the first kind can be planned and repaid.

howItWorks.title: Measure the interest, not the mess
howItWorks.text: In the model, a feature costs 10 points in clean code and one point more for every 10 points of debt. After 24 sprints of ignoring it, debt has grown from 30 to 120 and one feature costs 22 points instead of 10: the team has 45 features to show against 64 for the team that repaid in small steps. Interest is the extra cost per change, multiplied by how often that code changes. A real team can estimate it from how long changes in that area take against similar changes elsewhere.

howItWorks.title: Refactor in small steps, behind tests
howItWorks.text: Refactoring means changing structure without changing behaviour: rename, extract, move, inline. Each step is small enough to be undone, and a test run after it shows behaviour is unchanged. With tests, 8 points a sprint pays the debt down to 14 and delivers 64 features in 24 sprints. Without tests, every third sprint in the model leaks a regression costing 12 points, and the same plan delivers 57: still ahead, but only from sprint 14 instead of sprint 11, and with 8 regressions to explain. If there are no tests, first add characterization tests that pin down what the code does today.

howItWorks.title: Prefer small steps to a rewrite
howItWorks.text: A rewrite delivers nothing while it runs, has to rediscover every behaviour the old code had, and goes on collecting new rushed features with new debt. A 6-sprint rewrite in the model has 0 features after 6 sprints, 18 after 12, and 42 after 24: behind even doing nothing until sprint 28. A 12-sprint rewrite never catches up within 60 sprints. Rewrites that are staged and run alongside the old code, as in the strangler fig approach, keep delivering and keep the old behaviour as a reference.

howItWorks.title: Leave cold debt alone
howItWorks.text: If the messy code is never changed, nobody pays interest on it. In the model, with the debt in cold code a feature always costs 10, ignoring the debt delivers 96 features in 24 sprints, and every repayment plan delivers fewer: 72 for small steps, 72 for a 6-sprint rewrite. A stable module that works, has few readers and is never modified is not a priority just because it is ugly. Repay in the places the team keeps working in: the hot spots.

pros: Makes the trade-off visible: a deliberate shortcut is a decision with an owner and a repayment plan, not an accident
Keeps delivery speed from decaying: small repayments held at a steady rate keep the cost of a change flat
Small refactoring steps behind tests are safe, reversible and can be reviewed
Pointing at the interest in hot code gives a business reason for the work, not an aesthetic one
cons: Interest is hard to measure: the numbers in a model are tidy, a real code base is not
The metaphor is stretched to cover anything the team dislikes, and then every complaint becomes debt
Refactoring without tests can silently change behaviour, so the safety net often has to be built first
Repayment competes with features, and the benefit shows up later and spread across many changes
whenToUse: Code in the hot path of change, where every feature touches the same awkward module
Before adding a feature that will touch messy code, so the change itself becomes the small, safe step
After a deliberate shortcut was taken for a deadline: schedule the repayment while the reason is remembered
When estimates in one area are consistently higher than in similar areas of the system
whenNotToUse: Code that is stable and rarely changed: no interest is paid, so repaying costs more than it saves
Code you are about to delete or replace anyway, such as a feature being retired
As a license for rewrite proposals that stop delivery for several quarters without a staged plan
Untested code where you cannot tell whether behaviour changed: build the test net first, then refactor
pitfalls: Calling all code you dislike debt: a style you disagree with in a module nobody changes has no interest, and the label hides the real list
Refactoring without tests and without small steps, so a regression arrives with the clean-up and trust in the work is lost
Mixing a refactor and a behaviour change in one commit: when something breaks you cannot tell which step did it
Proposing a big rewrite because the old code is ugly: it stops delivery, rediscovers old bugs and creates new debt of its own
Never writing the debt down: a deliberate shortcut with no ticket, owner or reason becomes accidental debt within a few months
Paying down debt evenly across the code base instead of where the team works: the same hours buy much more in the hot spots
Treating a clean-up sprint as the plan: a steady share of every sprint beats a heroic quarter once a year that the next deadline erases

roles.label: Team
roles.description: Has 40 points of work per sprint to split between features and repayment.

roles.label: Hot code
roles.description: Changed every sprint, so debt here charges interest on every change.

roles.label: Cold code
roles.description: Untouched for a long time: ugly, but nobody pays for it.

roles.label: Test net
roles.description: Shows that a refactoring step changed structure and not behaviour.

roles.label: Rewrite
roles.description: A parallel replacement that delivers nothing until it is finished.

quiz.question: A module is ugly and hard to read, but nobody has changed it in two years and it has no known bugs. What does the debt metaphor say about it?
options: It should be refactored first, because the worst code carries the most debt.
It is a large debt, so a rewrite is the cheapest way to repay it.
It charges almost no interest, so repaying it is probably wasted effort.
It stops being debt only once a test suite covers every line in it.
quiz.explanation: Interest is the extra cost of each change, so debt in code nobody changes costs little. The same effort in the module changed every sprint buys far more. Untidiness alone is not the measure.

quiz.question: The team will refactor a module that has no tests. Which first step is safest?
options: Write tests that fix today's behaviour, then refactor in small steps.
Refactor it in one large change, then write tests against the new design.
Rewrite it from scratch so that the old behaviour no longer matters at all.
Refactor and add a feature in the same commit, to save the cost of a review.
quiz.explanation: Refactoring means changing structure while behaviour stays the same, and only a test run can show that. Characterization tests first, then small steps; mixing in a feature makes a regression impossible to place.

quiz.question: A 6-sprint rewrite starts in a team that otherwise ships 2 to 3 features per sprint. What does the simulation show about its first year?
options: It delivers faster from the start, because new code has no debt and no old workarounds at all.
It matches the old pace, as half the team keeps shipping features while the other half rewrites.
It ends the first two years ahead, because clean code is always faster to change than old code.
It ships nothing for 6 sprints, then trails the do-nothing team until about sprint 28.
quiz.explanation: A rewrite adds no features while it runs, and its new code collects rushed-feature debt again. In the model it trails the team that ignored the debt until sprint 28, and small steps do better throughout.
